take_homes: Two kinds of eval: one for the floor (is it grounded), one for the ceiling (did it do the job). We only have the floor kind.
A flat score tells you the judge ran out of things to see, not that the work is finished. And nobody has checked whether our judge agrees with a human.
Autonomy is a design decision per category of work: draft only, send to self, auto-send when the judges pass. Some categories always keep a human.

monday.move: Take one org-wide use case, sales follow-up mails, and put it in the judge-and-tactic loop. Before I trust the judge, I score about 15 outputs by hand and compare with it.
monday.who: Me, plus one person from sales to say what a good mail is. Not the whole sales team.
monday.when: Tuesday afternoon, after the weekend build. I'll put 'read one raw mail myself' in my calendar for every Friday.
monday.stop_condition: If the judge and my hand-scores disagree on more than about 3 in 10, I stop and fix the judge before any loop runs.
monday.blocker: Nobody in sales asked for this and I haven't settled who maintains the tactic file and the judge. Also, I will probably skip the hand-scoring and just build the loop.

misconception.why: 'A generator that grades itself passes itself' and 'every clean week erodes your ability to tell when the loop stops' hit the habit of skipping checks because the output looked fine. I now see a judge that nobody checked is still unchecked. I still think checking is mostly for the judge and not for every output, so I haven't changed my mind, only moved it a bit.

one_line: The loop part I could have built myself, but the floor-and-ceiling split and the line about checking the judge were new. The course should slow you down at that one point, and I skipped it anyway.
